code_scheme.format: T followed by four digits, one series across every dimension and the high-level classifications.
rules: A code identifies a concept, not a position. It is assigned the first time the concept appears in a transcribed version, and never renumbered or reused.
A concept keeps its code when it is renamed, moved to another dimension, or moved to another high-level classification. Only a split or merge creates new codes, and the new codes carry derived_from.
Codes are opaque on purpose. They say nothing about dimension or status, because both change between versions.
The EBA's PDF defines no codes. These are assigned by this repository. build/crosswalk-0.2.json maps the per-dimension codes of repository release 0.2 to these.

change_types.added: A new entry with no predecessor. Consumers add it.
change_types.retired: An entry removed with no successor. Its code is kept and never reused. Records classified under an earlier version stay valid under that version.
change_types.split: One entry replaced by several. Each successor carries derived_from; the retired predecessor carries superseded_by. Successors may sit in a different dimension from the predecessor. A trend series on the predecessor continues as the sum of its successors.
change_types.merged: Several entries replaced by one. The survivor carries derived_from listing each predecessor.
change_types.renamed: Same concept, different name. The code does not change, so stored records need no migration.
change_types.moved: Same concept, different dimension (for example a label/tag becoming a modus). The code does not change: codes are global, not per dimension. The entry carries moved_from.
change_types.regrouped: A modus moved to a different high-level classification. The code does not change; group_code does, and the entry carries regrouped_from.
change_types.redefined: The EBA declares that the definition was updated. The annex usually calls this a clarification, but it does not say whether the meaning changed, so treat stored records as needing review.
change_types.recited: The EBA declares that the definition was replaced with one from a different source. The EBA presents this as a change of source, not of meaning.
change_types.reworded: Observed only: the definition text differs between versions and the annex does not declare it. This repository cannot tell a cosmetic rewording from a change of meaning, and does not guess.
change_types.source_updated: Observed only: the definition text is unchanged but its cited source or link changed.
change_types.structure_changed: A change to the taxonomy's structure rather than to an entry: a dimension added, a chapter added or reordered, or a new attribute on every entry.

compatibility.principle: A record is classified under one version and carries that version. Consumers must expect records classified under a version other than the one they run, because the taxonomy is republished every June and adopters do not all move on the same day. The rules below let a consumer interpret such a record instead of rejecting it.
compatibility.code_stability: Because codes are global and follow the concept, a code read under any version means the same concept. What can differ between versions is where the concept sits (its dimension, its group) and what it is called. lineage.json records both for every version.

backward.meaning: A consumer on a newer version reading a record classified under an older version.
backward.rule: Resolve the record's codes against the version the record names. A code still present in the newer version is read directly, in whatever dimension it now sits. A retired code is found in the retired arrays; superseded_by gives its successors. Do not rewrite the stored record: interpret it, and keep the original version stamp.

forward.meaning: A consumer on an older version reading a record classified under a newer version.
forward.rule: An unrecognised code must not be discarded and must not be treated as invalid. Widen it: follow derived_from to a predecessor the consumer knows, and failing that fall back to the high-level classification, which is coarser but stable. Record that the value was widened.

compatibility.unknown_code_rule: Widen, never drop and never guess. Dropping an unknown code silently loses a case from every downstream count; guessing a sibling code invents data.

lossiness.exact: One code maps to one code. Safe in both directions. Includes renames and moves, which keep the code.
lossiness.widening: Several codes map to one coarser code. Safe: counts roll up without loss. This is the direction that keeps a trend series continuous across a split.
lossiness.narrowing: One code maps to several finer codes. Not automatically resolvable: the finer distinction was not in the original record. Keep the record at the coarser level or re-classify the case from its source material.

compatibility.dimension_moves: A move keeps the code but changes which field of a record the code belongs in. A record classified under 6.0 carries Romance fraud in labels_tags_codes; under 7.0 the same code is a modus. Reading the old record, keep the code where it was classified. Counting across versions, count the code, not the field.
compatibility.trend_series: To carry a series across a split, sum the successors and attribute the total to the predecessor. To carry it across a rename, a move or a regroup, do nothing: the code is unchanged.
compatibility.schema_versioning: Each version has its own schema.json, pinned to that version, so validation is unambiguous about what a record claims to be. Select the schema by the record's taxonomy_version field.

lifecycle_note: Every entry carries status, introduced_in and, where it changed, last_modified_in and last_change_type, plus renamed_from, moved_from, regrouped_from and derived_from where they apply. introduced_in is the first transcribed version in which the entry appears; '<=3.1' means it was already present in 3.1, the earliest public version. declared_introduced_in is set where the annex printed in 3.1 says the entry was added in 3.0. Retired entries keep their code and move to their dimension's retired array.
definitions_note: Definitions are the EBA's text, verbatim, with source attributions cut out into 'sources'. pdf_text holds the whole table cell exactly as extracted, including the attribution, so every definition can be checked against it. Where the EBA quotes a third party, the quotation marks and ellipses are the EBA's. Line breaks are collapsed and URLs the PDF wrapped are re-joined; nothing else is changed. The PDF governs.

modus.label: Modus (what)
modus.definition: Describes the unauthorised and often manipulative action taken by the fraudster and resulting in the loss of money via a payment transaction

high_level_classifications.name: Your money is at risk
high_level_classifications.definition: Fraudster tricks victim into believing their money is not safe where it currently is.

modi.name: Safe account fraud
modi.definition: The fraudster impersonates a bank or police representative and asks bank customer to transfer money from his/her payment account to a ‘safe account’. Alternatively, this modus could result in the victim handing over account credentials or card details and/or completing authentication steps required to access the account and/or sign off payment transactions.

values.name: Fraudulent use of Contract for Difference (CFD)
values.definition: “A contract for difference (CFD) is a popular type of derivative in finance. Derivatives are time-limited contracts that ‘derive’ their value from the market performance of an asset. CFDs allow you to speculate on various financial markets, including stocks, indices, commodities, forex pairs, and cryptocurrencies. You never buy the assets but trade on the rise or fall in their price, usually over a short period of time. A CFD is a contract between a broker and a trader who agree to exchange the difference in value of an underlying security between the beginning and the end of the contract, often less than one day.”

examples: Fraudster pretends to represent a legitimate company offering an investment opportunity based on CFD. The customer is directed to a fake website where he/she is tricked into setting up an account. Once the customer wishes to liquidate the account, the funds are gone.

values.name: Lookalike domain
values.definition: “Lookalike or ‘cousin’ domain names are addresses that use character replacement to make them look as close as possible to the domain of a brand, service or government authority. For example, characters in a domain name such as an “I” can be replaced with a “1”, or the letter l with the number 1. These names are most often registered by third parties up to mischief. introduction.heading: Introduction to the EBA Fraud Taxonomy
introduction.text:
Background
Stepping up pan-European co-operation to fight and prevent payment fraud has become a key priority among fraud experts in the growing real-
time payments ecosystem. The Euro Banking Association (EBA) created the Expert Group on Payment Fraud-related Topics (EGPF) in February
2020 to work towards a collaborative approach to fraud-combatting in the pan-European payments industry. The objectives of the EGPF are to
analyse minimum requirements for enabling a pan-European fraud intelligence approach and to define what fraud information and data could be
exchanged as part of this approach. To facilitate the work on these matters, the EGPF also looked into the development of a common vocabulary
in relation to payment fraud-related topics, to serve in a pan-European context.
When considering the best way forward to structure the data and intelligence that should ideally be shared to effectively detect and prevent
payment fraud, the EGPF concluded that the fraud type was the most important variable driving the need for specific data input. Since no uniform
set of definitions of fraud types had previously been agreed at a pan-European level, the EGPF determined to develop, in a first step, a joint
approach to fraud type categorisation.
Structure of the taxonomy
The present EBA Fraud Taxonomy (joint approach to fraud type categorisation) focuses on identifying the following elements relevant to a
fraudulent action: initiator (who), method (how), modus (what) and labels/tags; the latter can be freely chosen by individual payment service
providers (PSPs) and allows them to enrich the case with additional categorisation information on a voluntary basis.
This fraud taxonomy has been designed to meet the following objectives:
• Aligning with the European Banking Authority (EBA) Guidelines on Fraud Reporting under PSD2, which have already been implemented
by PSPs across Europe.
• Reducing the risk of overlap in the identification of fraud types and, consequently, increasing the accuracy of statistics used to identify
fraud trends.
• Facilitating a standardised means to (a) describe the attack vector and specify the first point of contact between the fraudster and the
victim (“how”) and (b) describe the unauthorised and often manipulative action taken by the fraudster and resulting in the loss of money
via a payment transaction (“what”).
• Ensuring that individual PSPs remain free to choose labels/tags for specific fraud scenarios as they deem fit, for example to align with
internal reporting requirements.
• Providing definitions based on authoritative and publicly available sources for the different modi and labels, wherever possible.
2
Publication history
The EBA released version 2.0 of the EBA Fraud Taxonomy in July 2021 to the financial institutions in the Association’s membership for a first
try-out phase with the aim to gather practical experience in deploying a uniform taxonomy at pan-European level. To ensure that the EBA Fraud
Taxonomy evolves in line with latest insights provided by fraud experts on how to effectively categorise fraud types, it is subject to an annual
review and updating process.
On 15 October 2021, the EBA launched the first annual change cycle with a call for change requests to the Association’s Member
Representatives. The first round of the review and updating process led to the release of version 3.0 of the EBA Fraud Taxonomy in June 2022.
This allows users to deploy the updated version of the taxonomy by the end of December 2022 for implementation effective on 1 January 2023.
An overview of the changes introduced into version 3.0 of the EBA Fraud Taxonomy compared to the version 2.0 is set out in the Annex of this
document.
Following the first try-out phase of the EBA Fraud Taxonomy and the closing of the first annual change cycle, the EBA Fraud Taxonomy shall
classify as a public document under an updated usage rights regime. The EBA released version 3.1 of the EBA Fraud Taxonomy in October
2022, containing changes to the introduction (only) of the EBA Fraud Taxonomy to bring clarity on the usage rights ahead of 1 January 2023,
when version 3.1 will come into effect.
Purpose and usage rights
The EBA Fraud Taxonomy could be used by PSPs and other stakeholders in different ways as they see fit depending on their needs, and could
help to streamline fraud categorisation, fraud reporting, and payment fraud-related data and intelligence sharing. It also supports PSPs in
developing effective measures against payment fraud that can be communicated to customers with a view to better protecting them.
The EBA Fraud Taxonomy by the Euro Banking Association is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International Public License
(CC BY 4.0 license).
Use of the EBA Fraud Taxonomy further entails:
•
acknowledgement of the review and updating process of the EBA Fraud Taxonomy, and acknowledgement of the expectation
that updated versions should be implemented by users effective on 1 January following the completion of an annual review
cycle, save in case of emergency updates which may require implementation on another date; and
•
adherence to the objective to create a common vocabulary for fraud types at a pan-European level without limitations on the
type of payment instrument.

• “Unauthorised payment transactions made, including as a result of the loss, theft or misappropriation of sensitive payment data or a

review_and_updating_process.heading: Review and updating process
review_and_updating_process.text:
1. Annual change cycle
To ensure that the EBA Fraud Taxonomy evolves in line with latest insights provided by fraud experts on how to effectively categorise fraud
types, it is subject to a review and updating process. Changes to the EBA Fraud Taxonomy are agreed once annually based on the following
process:
• Consultation process – second week of October: the EBA invites change requests from EGPF members, fraud experts of EBA member
organisations and organisations that have usage rights on the fraud taxonomy. Any party wishing to introduce a change request must use a
standard form made available by the EBA. Each change request must specify the reason for the suggested change.
• Submission of change requests:
o Second week of January: deadline to submit change requests pertaining to the ‘initiator’, ‘method’ and ‘modus’ sections of the EBA
Fraud Taxonomy. The specific deadline to submit a change request will be agreed by the EGPF each year.
o Early April: deadline to submit change requests pertaining to the ‘labels/tags’ section. A related change request must specify the
proposed naming and definition of the new label.
• Review process – mid-January to mid-April: the EGPF reviews the change requests received. Organisations that have submitted change
requests, but are currently not members of the EGPF, will be invited to join the relevant EGPF meeting to engage in the review process.
Following review, the EGPF will recommend an updated version of the EBA Fraud Taxonomy.
• Adoption of updated version of EBA Fraud Taxonomy – May: the EBA Board adopts an updated version of EBA Fraud Taxonomy.
• Communication of updated version of EBA fraud taxonomy – June: the EBA communicates an updated version of the EBA Fraud
Taxonomy to EGPF members, fraud experts of EBA member organisations and organisations that have usage rights on the fraud taxonomy.
• Implementation of updated version of EBA Fraud Taxonomy by users – deployment by end of December for implementation
effective on 1 January of the next calendar year: users are provided with a six-month lead-time to implement an updated version of the
EBA Fraud Taxonomy.
2. Emergency change process
If exceptional circumstances require immediate amendments to the EBA Fraud Taxonomy, the emergency change process applies. In this case,
the steps leading to the adoption of an updated version of the EBA Fraud Taxonomy may be expedited as required. The emergency change
process is triggered if and when considered necessary or appropriate; by way of illustration, circumstances that could trigger an emergency
change process could for example include, but are not limited to, regulatory requirements that point to the need to align the taxonomy in an
expedited manner, or payment fraud-related developments with a high degree of proliferation and a potential large-scale impact.

The classification of the EBA Fraud Taxonomy was changed from ‘closed user group’ to ‘public’.
The copyright notice was amended to reference the CC BY 4.0 license.
Amendments in the chapter ‘Introduction to the EBA Fraud Taxonomy’:
• Publication history: a paragraph was added to cover the update through version 3.1 to bring clarity on the accessibility and usage
rights regime ahead of 1 January 2023.

o Reference to the licensing under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International Public License (CC BY 4.0 license)
o Clarification added that use of the EBA Fraud Taxonomy further entails acknowledgement of the expectation that the latest
version is implemented by all users, and adherence to the objective to create a common vocabulary for fraud types at a pan-
European level without limitation on the type of payment instrument
